opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, it's a pleasure to be here.

The basic idea goes back to around 1990, when I started building artificial curious agents. The question was: how can you motivate a learning system to explore the world in a sensible way, even when there is no external reward, no teacher telling it what to do? My answer was to give the agent an intrinsic reward for improving its own predictions or compressions of the incoming data.

So imagine you have two modules. One is a world model, a predictor that tries to model and compress the history of observations and actions. The other is a controller, a reinforcement learner that chooses actions. The controller gets intrinsic reward whenever the world model *improves*, whenever it learns something that makes the data more compressible than before. In the formal version, the reward is the compression progress: the number of bits saved by the improved model.

The crucial point is that the reward is not for things that are predictable, and not for things that are random. Something already fully predictable is boring, because there is nothing left to learn. Pure noise is also boring, because no matter how hard you try, you cannot compress it. What is interesting is the stuff in between: data that has a regularity you don't yet know but *can* learn. That's where the first derivative of compressibility is positive, and that's where curiosity drives you.

I think this simple principle explains a lot about science, art, and humor. Consider a physicist. Before Newton, you have lots of observations of falling apples and planetary orbits, and they take many bits to store. Then someone discovers a simple law, and suddenly the whole history of observations becomes much more compressible. That is a huge compression progress, a huge "aha" moment, and the scientist experiences it as joy, as fun. The same is true for Kepler, for Einstein, and also, on a much smaller scale, for a baby who learns that dropped objects fall down.

Art and music are similar. A good piece of music is neither entirely predictable nor random. The listener discovers a novel pattern, a theme and its variations, and the internal compressor gets better at encoding it. That learning process is subjectively beautiful, or interesting. Even a joke works this way: the punchline lets you reinterpret the setup in an unexpected but more compressed manner.

And of course this is not just philosophy. We implemented it in artificial systems, starting with those early adversarial setups where the controller tries to generate experiments that the world model cannot yet predict, which in a way anticipated later generative adversarial ideas. The broader point is that a creative scientist, or an artificial scientist, is basically a system that invents its own experiments to discover new, learnable regularities, and gets rewarded for the progress in understanding. That, I would argue, is the essence of curiosity, and it's what will drive the artificial scientists of the future.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists invent experiments, but it does not identify inventing good questions as part of scientific work.

r002.rationale: It describes interesting data as a learnable regularity the scientist does not yet know, between what is already predictable and pure noise.

r003.rationale: It explains that discovering a simple law makes the observations more compressible.

r004.rationale: It links learning that improves compression to joy and fun.

r005.rationale: It says the controller chooses actions and receives intrinsic reward when the world model improves through compression progress.

r006.rationale: It calls fully predictable things boring because there is nothing left to learn.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic idea is very simple, and I have been saying this since 1990 or so. Curiosity is not some mysterious thing. It is what happens when a learning agent is rewarded for improving its own model of the world.

Think of a little agent in the world. It observes things, it acts, and all the time it is trying to compress its history of observations. It builds a predictive model, a compressor. Now, most of the world is either boring because it is already predictable, or boring because it is random noise that you can never predict. Neither of those is interesting. A white wall is boring. Static on a television screen is also boring, even though it is completely unpredictable.

What is interesting is the stuff in between: data that is not yet compressible, but that contains some regularity you are about to discover. So in my formal theory, the intrinsic reward, the fun, is the first derivative of compression progress. It is not how well you predict the world, it is how much better your predictions become over time, how many bits you save as you learn. The agent has a second module, a reinforcement learner, which is rewarded for steering the agent toward situations where the model expects to make such progress. That is curiosity. The agent actively seeks out the novel patterns it can learn, and it loses interest once they are learned, because then there is no more progress to be had.

And this one principle explains a surprising amount. A scientist is a system that gets intrinsic reward from finding simple laws that compress many observations. Newton saw apples falling and planets orbiting and found one formula, enormous compression progress, and that felt wonderful. Art is similar: a composer or a painter creates data that is novel but learnable. Humor, too: a joke sets up an expectation and then reveals a shorter explanation you did not see coming, and that sudden compression is funny. Even what we call beauty tends to be what is subjectively compressible given the observer's history, for example faces that are close to the average of faces you have seen.

So scientific curiosity, in this view, is the drive to go where your current world model is about to get noticeably shorter. And of course we built artificial agents with exactly this kind of reward signal, already in the early nineties, with a predictor and a controller, and later versions with proper compression progress measures. They explore not randomly but in a focused way, toward what is learnable. That is a much more principled explanation of why anyone would bother to do science at all, rather than just maximizing external reward.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity and scientific discovery, but does not identify inventing good questions as part of scientific work.

r002.rationale: It says curiosity seeks “novel patterns” the agent can learn and describes interesting data as containing regularity “you are about to discover.”

r003.rationale: It explains that finding a simple law compresses many observations, and describes learning as saving bits in the model.

r004.rationale: It explicitly defines intrinsic reward or “fun” as the first derivative of compression progress—how much better predictions become over time.

r005.rationale: It says a reinforcement learner is rewarded for steering the agent toward situations where the model expects compression progress, and calls this a controller.

r006.rationale: It states that the agent “loses interest once they are learned” because no further progress remains.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that curiosity is driven by progress in understanding. Imagine that you have a predictive model of the world. As you observe things, you try to find regularities that allow you to predict them better—or, equivalently, to compress your observations into a shorter description. The fun comes when that model improves.

This distinguishes something that is merely surprising from something that is interesting. A completely predictable situation is boring because there is nothing left to learn. But random noise is also boring, once you recognize that you cannot learn to predict it. The interesting situations are those where you do not yet understand the regularity, but you can make progress toward discovering it.

You can formalize this with two components: a learner that improves its model, and a controller that chooses actions or experiments. The controller receives an intrinsic reward for the learner’s measurable improvement. So it learns to seek out situations in which learning pays off.

A scientist does something similar: choosing an experiment that might reveal a previously hidden regularity. When a simple law suddenly explains many observations, that is a big improvement in compression. The pleasure of that discovery is what the theory tries to capture—not how much you already know, but how much better you are becoming at understanding.

r001.rationale: It describes choosing experiments, but does not identify inventing good questions as part of scientific work.

r002.rationale: It says curiosity seeks hidden regularities that can be learned, but does not specify that they are readily learnable from the scientist’s current understanding.

r003.rationale: It explains that regularities let observations be compressed into a shorter description.

r004.rationale: It links fun to a learner’s improving model and describes discovery as a compression improvement.

r005.rationale: It says the controller receives intrinsic reward for the learner’s measurable improvement, which the response connects to improved compression.

r006.rationale: It describes a completely predictable situation as boring because nothing remains to learn.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that a curious scientist seeks situations where there is something new to learn—not merely something unpredictable. We can formalize this with two systems: a predictor, or compressor, that tries to find regularities in the history of observations, and a controller that chooses actions. The controller receives an intrinsic reward whenever the predictor improves.

Suppose you watch a completely predictable sequence. You already understand it, so there is no progress and it becomes boring. Now suppose you watch pure random noise. You cannot discover a useful regularity, so that also becomes boring. The interesting things lie in between: things you do not yet understand, but where you can make progress.

In this view, the joy of discovery is the pleasure of improved compression. Previously, you needed many separate facts to describe your observations; suddenly, you discover a simple rule that explains them. A scientist chooses experiments that may produce such improvements. An artist can create experiences that allow an audience to discover new structure. Both are connected by the same principle: we are interested in what lets us improve our understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists choose experiments, but does not identify inventing good questions as part of scientific work.

r002.rationale: It describes seeking something new to learn rather than pure unpredictability, and says the interesting cases are not yet understood but allow progress through discovering regularities.

r003.rationale: It explains that a simple rule can replace many separate facts in describing observations.

r004.rationale: It identifies the joy of discovery with the pleasure of improved compression.

r005.rationale: It says the controller chooses actions and receives intrinsic reward whenever the predictor improves.

r006.rationale: It says a completely predictable sequence is already understood and becomes boring.
